edges.description: T-cell predominant autoimmune activation drives cellular infiltration into the vitreous cavity.
Chronic T-cell inflammation at the pars plana leads to post-inflammatory glial proliferation of fibrous astrocytes forming snowbanks.
Intraocular inflammation in pars planitis is frequently accompanied by peripheral retinal vasculitis and venular sheathing.
Intraocular inflammation in pars planitis frequently produces angiographic or clinical optic disc edema.
Chronic intraocular inflammation in pars planitis frequently leads to complicated cataract formation.
Severe or prolonged intraocular inflammation in pars planitis can rarely be followed by progressive intraretinal bone-spicule pigmentation mimicking retinitis pigmentosa.
Aggregation of inflammatory cells in the mid-vitreous and inferior peripheral vitreous forms yellow-white snowball opacities.
Vitreous inflammatory cells and snowball opacities are associated with presenting floater symptoms.
Vitreous inflammation and haze contribute to blurred vision at presentation.
Aggregation of floaters in the vitreous can cause significant visual loss in severe cases.
Exudative snowbanks on the inferior pars plana and associated vitreous base inflammation accompany characteristic vitreous opacities.
Retinal vascular inflammation and perivasculitis are evaluated alongside cystoid macular edema on fluorescein angiography.

nodes.description: Pars planitis shows a T cell-driven autoimmune response within the vitreous and pars plana.

evidence.reference_title: Immunopathogenic Background of Pars Planitis.
evidence.snippet: Clinical and histopathological findings suggest an autoimmune etiology, most likely as a reaction to endogenous antigen of unknown source, with T cells predominant in both vitreous and pars plana infiltrations.

evidence.reference_title: Pediatric Pars Planitis: A Review.
evidence.snippet: Pars planitis refers to the idiopathic subset of intermediate uveitis in which there is vitritis along with snowball or snowbank formation occurring in the absence of an associated infection or systemic disease. It is thought to be a T-cell mediated disease with a genetic predisposition.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical characteristics and treatment of pars planitis: an adalimumab experience.
evidence.snippet: ADA was initiated in 23 patients (38.9%) due to refractory uveitis and adverse effects to the corticosteroid and helped control intraocular inflammation and decrease the use of systemic steroids/immunosuppressives in 22 of 23 (95%) of patients who received ADA.

evidence.reference_title: Pars Planitis: Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, Management and Visual Prognosis.
evidence.snippet: The most common symptoms at presentation are floaters and blurred vision. Donaldson et al reported blurred vision in 74% and floaters in 61% of cases at the time of diagnosis.

evidence.reference_title: Pars Planitis: Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, Management and Visual Prognosis.
evidence.snippet: Prieto et al showed even higher rates of blurred vision (81.8%), while floaters were rarely reported (9%).

evidence.reference_title: Pars Planitis: Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, Management and Visual Prognosis.
evidence.snippet: In the majority of studies, cataracts were the most frequent reported complication of pars planitis occurring at high rates ranging from 30.4% to 47.5%.

evidence.reference_title: Pars Planitis: Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, Management and Visual Prognosis.
evidence.snippet: A stepladder approach including corticosteroids, immunosupressive agents, anti-tumor necrosis factor-alpha and pars plana vitrectomy and/or laser photocoagulation is the most commonly used method for treatment of pars planitis.

evidence.reference_title: Pars Planitis: Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, Management and Visual Prognosis.
evidence.snippet: Donaldson et al observed epiretinal membranes in 36.9% of subjects as the most common complication in their series, followed by cataract (30.4%) and cystoid macular edema (26%). Epiretinal membrane formation was found to be directly related to disease chronicity, and the mean interval between disease onset and epiretinal membrane formation was 7.9 years.

evidence.reference_title: Analysis of clinical features and visual outcomes of pars planitis.
evidence.snippet: Vitreous inflammation (100%), vitreous haze (92.6%), snowballs (74.1%), snowbanks (66.7%), anterior chamber cells (66.7%) and peripheral retinal vascular sheathing (48.1%) were the most common presentations.

evidence.reference_title: Progression of retinal pigmentation mimicking unilateral retinitis pigmentosa after bilateral pars planitis: a case report.
evidence.snippet: He was diagnosed with bilateral pars planitis. Progressive, intraretinal bone crepuscule pigmentation developed in his left retina during the following three months. An electroretinogram showed subnormal response only in the left eye, suggesting the diagnosis of unilateral pseudoRP.
